traces.question: Given the setup for the Au film sample, look at the cross-section SEM panel from Figure 1 (F1b) of the annealed film. What does the image show about how a single grain relates to the film thickness across the field of view, and what does this establish about the overall shape of the grains?

traces.question: Given the context above, look at panel F4a, which overlays the grain's measured heating/cooling branches against the response predicted from simple elastic behavior under the applied thermal loading. How do the measured branches compare to that predicted response - do they track it, exceed it, or fall well short - and roughly by what factor? What does this comparison suggest about how much internal strain variation the coherent-diffraction method can reveal within a single grain over a full cycle?
traces.answer_key: None of the measured branches matches the straight-line response predicted by simple elastic behavior under the applied thermal loading; that predicted reference is about three times steeper than any of the measured cycles (o8). Instead, the grain's measured strain traces a loop running from about -0.05% to about -0.17% over one cycle, far shallower than the reference (a15). This shows the method can follow a single buried grain through a full thermal cycle and recover both its average strain and its 3-D displacement field (a19), supporting the conclusion that the grain carries large, anisotropic, quasi-reversible internal strain heterogeneities set by its immediate neighbourhood - heterogeneities invisible to averaged diffraction (a20).
traces.grading: Answer key: the numbers and labels on the evidence node o8 (the roughly three-times-steeper reference slope and the mismatch of all branches), plus the claim a15 (the -0.05% to -0.17% loop) and the downstream nodes a19 and a20, judge-confirmed against the panel F4a reading.

traces.question: Panels F6a-F6e give the five diffraction-derived strain images of the single grain across the thermal cycle, alongside the context on how the grain was grown and imaged. From those panels alone, how does the spatial pattern of internal strain within the grain change as the temperature is raised, along which directions does it develop, and what happens to it once the sample cools back down?
traces.answer_key: The strain distribution stays even through the film thickness (z) at all stages shown. In the plane of the film it is dominated by variation along y at 50 C, then reorganizes into jumps along x by 240 C, and on cooling most of that x-direction pattern reverts (o13). This underlies the claim that the intra-grain heterogeneity is strongly anisotropic and grows with temperature, developing along x in-plane while staying weak through the thickness (a16), a change that is quasi-reversible rather than a permanent plastic shift (a17), reflecting the method's ability to track one buried grain's average strain and 3-D displacement field through a full thermal cycle (a19), and supporting the conclusion that a single grain carries large, anisotropic, quasi-reversible intra-granular strain set by its immediate neighbourhood that averaged diffraction cannot see (a20).
traces.grading: Independent channel o12 (DERIVED), held out from the model: the size-only broadening value (6.61e-4 A^-1, two to seven times smaller than the measured qx widths) is checked against the anisotropy the model reads from the panels, without ever being shown to it.

traces.question: Using the setup above (buried grain, thermal cycling, and the diffraction method meant to resolve the grain's internal displacement field), look at panels F6a through F6e, which follow that grain across the temperature series. How does the pattern of intra-grain variation change along the film's in-plane directions versus through its thickness as temperature rises, and what happens to that pattern once the sample is cooled back down? What does this imply about whether the underlying deformation is permanent or not, and what capability and broader conclusion about single-grain behavior does this support?
traces.answer_key: Through the film thickness (z) the maps stay uniform at every temperature. In the plane, the variation is dominated by one direction at 50 C, then breaks into jumps along the other in-plane direction by 240 C, and largely returns to its original pattern on cooling (o13). Because the heterogeneity mostly reverses on cooling rather than staying permanently changed, the behavior is judged quasi-reversible, i.e. anelastic rather than truly plastic (a17). This supports that the method can follow one buried grain through a full thermal cycle and report both its average strain and its 3-D displacement field (a19), and it leads to the broader conclusion that a single grain carries large, anisotropic, quasi-reversible intra-granular strain heterogeneities set by its immediate neighbourhood, heterogeneities invisible to diffraction that only averages over many grains (a20).
traces.grading: Answer key: the numbers and labels on the evidence and downstream nodes o13, a17, a19, a20, judge-confirmed against the trace's stated grader.

traces.question: Panels F6a-F6e are the coherent X-ray diffraction images described in the context above, taken on the single Au grain from a10 across the temperature series set up in a1/a2, probing the anisotropic intra-grain heterogeneity of a16 and its reversibility described in a17. Reading the five panels in order from the lowest to the highest temperature and back down again, how does the spatial pattern of the variation within the grain change with temperature, and what happens to it once the sample cools?
traces.answer_key: The images stay uniform through the film thickness (along z) at every temperature. In-plane, the variation is dominated by one direction (y) at 50 C, then breaks into jumps along the other in-plane direction (x) by 240 C, and largely returns to its earlier pattern on cooling (o13). This is what lets the method track one specific embedded grain across the whole temperature run and report both its average strain and its complete 3-D displacement field (a19). Together this shows that a single grain carries large, direction-dependent, and largely-recoverable internal strain variation set by its immediate surroundings, a level of detail that diffraction methods averaging over many grains cannot see (a20).

traces.question: The context above shows intra-grain strain heterogeneity building up strongly along x in the film plane while staying weak through the thickness, and growing with temperature. Two competing causes are given along with their evidence: the columnar grain structure (cross-section SEM) and defect storage from thermal loading, preferentially along x. Which cause accounts for this x-specific, temperature-growing pattern, and by what mechanism does it produce it?
traces.answer_key: The columnar-grain cause is the one that explains it. Its neighbouring grains g3 and g6, which are misoriented and lie along x, meet at grooved boundaries; those boundaries accommodate stress and trap defects there, and that is what builds up the x-direction heterogeneity while the through-thickness direction, lacking such boundaries, stays weak (a18). The rival cause, thermal-loading defect storage, has no evidence tied to any stated optimum, unlike the columnar-grain cause whose cross-section evidence (o1) is most developed exactly at the claim's optimum -- so the rival cannot on its own be shown to set the x-specific pattern.
traces.grading: Judge against the graph's explaining mechanism a18 as the key, cross-checked by the fact that the rival cause a14 has no evidence establishing an optimum while the accepted cause a10's evidence (o1) matches the claim's optimum.
